title: Mark 15:21–32
context: Mark’s account of the crucifixion is spare and restrained. A passerby, Simon of Cyrene, is forced to carry the cross. At Golgotha Jesus refuses drugged wine, the soldiers divide his clothes, and the charge “THE KING OF THE JEWS” is posted above him between two robbers. Passersby, chief priests, and even the men crucified with him mock him: “He saved others. He can’t save himself.” Both traditions see the deep irony: by not saving himself, Jesus saves others. Verse 28 is missing from many early manuscripts and is omitted from some modern editions; the WEB includes it with a note.

verses.text: They compelled one passing by, coming from the country, Simon of Cyrene, the father of Alexander and Rufus, to go with them that he might bear his cross.
verses.arminianNotes: Simon of Cyrene, from North Africa, is forced to carry the cross. Mark names his sons Alexander and Rufus, probably because Mark’s readers knew them (compare Romans 16:13, though the identification is uncertain). Arminian readers see a man drawn unexpectedly into Jesus’ story.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers often see God’s providence even in this forced labor. Both traditions find here a picture of discipleship: taking up the cross behind Jesus (Mark 8:34).

verses.text: They brought him to the place called Golgotha, which is, being interpreted, “The place of a skull.”
verses.arminianNotes: Golgotha means “the place of a skull.” Arminian readers note Mark’s care to translate for his non-Aramaic readers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same. The exact location is a historical question, not a theological one.

verses.text: They offered him wine mixed with myrrh to drink, but he didn’t take it.
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus refuses wine mixed with myrrh, probably offered to dull the pain. Arminian readers see Jesus choosing to face his suffering fully aware.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a willing acceptance of the cup the Father had given him (Mark 14:36). Both traditions read this as a sign of his deliberate obedience.

verses.text: Crucifying him, they parted his garments among them, casting lots on them, what each should take.
verses.arminianNotes: The soldiers crucify him and gamble for his clothes, echoing Psalm 22:18. Arminian readers note that the psalm of the righteous sufferer shapes the scene.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see fulfilled Scripture and God’s purpose at work. Both traditions read Psalm 22 as a key to Mark’s account, which reaches its peak in verse 34.

verses.text: It was the third hour when they crucified him.
verses.arminianNotes: Mark places the crucifixion at the third hour, about 9 a.m. John 19:14 places a stage of the trial around the sixth hour, a known difficulty that interpreters handle in several ways. Arminian readers note the question honestly without forcing a single solution.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also acknowledge the difficulty and offer various harmonizations, such as different ways of reckoning time. Neither tradition treats this question as a dividing line.

verses.text: The superscription of his accusation was written over him: “THE KING OF THE JEWS.”
verses.arminianNotes: The written charge reads “THE KING OF THE JEWS.” Arminian readers note that Rome’s mockery announces the truth.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s irony: the cross proclaims Christ’s kingship. Both traditions hear the title as true in a way its authors never intended.

verses.text: With him they crucified two robbers, one on his right hand, and one on his left.
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus is crucified between two robbers, perhaps rebels like Barabbas. Arminian readers see him placed among sinners in death.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also see him counted with the guilty, an image of substitution often linked to Isaiah 53:12. Both traditions note Mark’s restraint in describing it.

verses.text: The Scripture was fulfilled which says, “He was counted with transgressors.”
verses.arminianNotes: This verse quotes Isaiah 53:12, “He was counted with transgressors.” It is missing from the earliest manuscripts and is omitted from many modern critical editions; the WEB includes it and notes the omission. Arminian readers note that the idea is fully biblical (Luke 22:37), whatever its place in Mark.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers make the same point: the textual question does not affect doctrine, since Luke 22:37 records Jesus applying Isaiah 53:12 to himself. Both traditions treat it as an honest textual question.

verses.text: Those who passed by blasphemed him, wagging their heads and saying, “Ha! You who destroy the temple and build it in three days,
verses.arminianNotes: Passersby mock him, wagging their heads (Psalm 22:7), and twist his words about the temple. Arminian readers note how misunderstanding his claims leads to scorn.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the irony: the true temple is about to be destroyed and raised in three days. Both traditions see the mockers saying more than they understand.

verses.text: save yourself, and come down from the cross!”
verses.arminianNotes: “Save yourself, and come down from the cross!” Arminian readers see the final temptation to take a path without suffering.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same temptation, echoing Peter’s rebuke in Mark 8:32–33. Both traditions agree that by staying on the cross, Jesus chose obedience.

verses.text: Likewise, also the chief priests mocking among themselves with the scribes said, “He saved others. He can’t save himself.
verses.arminianNotes: “He saved others. He can’t save himself.” The leaders speak deeper truth than they know. Arminian readers stress that Jesus could have saved himself but freely chose not to, out of love for others.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree that his “cannot” is a matter of obedience to the Father’s will, not lack of power: to save others, he would not save himself. Both traditions see the gospel’s heart in this taunt.

verses.text: Let the Christ, the King of Israel, now come down from the cross, that we may see and believe him.” Those who were crucified with him also insulted him.
verses.arminianNotes: The leaders demand a sign: come down, and “we will believe.” Even those crucified with him insult him. Arminian readers note that demanding signs on one’s own terms is not true faith.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers make the same point, noting that faith comes not from such signs but from God’s work in the heart. Both traditions see the scene as the depth of Jesus’ rejection.
